hints: Notice the wire narrows from area $A$ at R to $\frac{1}{2}A$ at S, but it is one continuous series conductor with a constant current.
Recall $I = Q/t$, so the charge passing a point in time $t$ depends only on $I$, and charge cannot build up inside the wire.
Ask what must change at S to keep $I$ the same through the smaller area - drift speed, not charge per second.
walkthrough: Identify the setup: a single wire with cross-section $A$ at point R narrowing to $\frac{1}{2}A$ at point S, carrying one constant current.
State the governing rule: current is rate of flow of charge, $I = Q/t$, and in a series conductor the current is the same at every cross-section because charge is conserved.
Use the given data at R: charge $Q$ passes in time $t$, so $I = Q/t$ throughout the wire.
Explain the effect of the smaller area: from $I = nAvq$, the mean drift speed $v$ must be larger at S to carry the same $I$ through area $\frac{1}{2}A$, but $I$ itself is unchanged.
Apply the same $I$ at S for the same time $t$: charge at S $= It = (Q/t) \times t = Q$. This is option B.

options.A: Charge is not proportional to area $A$. Halving the area does not halve the charge passing per second in a series wire.
options.B: Current is the same everywhere in a single wire, so $Q = It$ is the same at R and at S in the same time $t$.
options.C: The factor $\sqrt{2}$ has no role here. Charge conservation does not involve a square root of the area ratio.
options.D: Charge does not double when area halves. The drift speed increases, but the rate of charge flow stays constant.
